# Characters — THE CONDITION REPORT

---

## 1. Sebastiaan Corvelijn — the darker lead

**Age 41.** Sole partner and *bewindvoerder* of Corvelijn & Zonen,
Kloosterstraat 118, Antwerp. Nine years in the chair. Adult status
established chapter 2: forty-one, divorced from Meike in 2018, has run a
six-person firm since his father's death in 2016.

**Appearance.** Tall, narrow through the shoulders, grey at the temples
early and unbothered by it. A conservator's hands on a dealer's body:
short nails, one permanent ink callus on the middle finger of the right
hand. Wears the same four suits in rotation, none of them new, all of them
correct, and a coat he has had since 2009 and has had relined twice rather
than replace. Reading glasses he refuses to wear in front of clients, so he
holds documents at arm's length in meetings and everyone thinks it is
disdain.

### Ghost → Wound → Lie → Want → Need

**GHOST.** October 1997, aged nineteen, home from his first term. His
father Lucien asked him to hold a lamp in the back room. Sebastiaan held it
for two hours while Lucien made a 1938 Reich export stamp on a piece of
1930s laid paper, and then Armand Brassart came at eight in the evening and
signed the report that said it was period. Sebastiaan cut the paper to size
because his hands were steadier. He was not tricked and he was not coerced.
He was pleased to be asked.

**WOUND.** He believes he is not a person who has a business, but the
current instalment of a fraud — that the firm and he are the same object,
and that if the fraud is ever named, everything back to 1951 becomes a crime
retrospectively, including the sixty families currently waiting for their
pictures. He has never said this out loud to anyone.

**LIE, in one sentence.** *A thing is only false once someone withdraws it;
nothing filed can be unfiled, therefore nothing filed is a lie.*

This is not a philosophical position, it is a procedural one, and it is
almost true. Article 11 says the docket is append-only. He has built a
whole ethics out of an administrative rule. It lets him hold the 1997 report
in a drawer for six years without being a blackmailer, because he has never
used it; it lets him forge a signature in chapter 4 without being a forger,
because the document is now simply a fact of the record.

**TRUTH (his Need).** A thing is false the moment it is untrue, and the
only person who can say so is the person who signed it. He does not need to
be forgiven and he does not need to be loved. **He needs to withdraw
something** — to be the author of a subtraction rather than only ever of
additions. Until chapter 33 he has never in his life taken anything back.

**WANT.** Close the Schindler-Wolff Zurich claim before the reckoning on 31
March, clear the €4.1 million, and hold the claim book. Stated flat in
chapter 2, before Lena is anything to him. **This want exists independently
of her and survives her: in chapter 30, with her gone, he is still working
the claim.**

**Want vs Need in tension:** the Want requires him to keep adding to the
record — filings, annexes, reports, one of them in her name. The Need
requires him to take something off it. He cannot do both. In chapter 29 he
chooses the Want, in the most explicit terms available, and names her as the
forger. In chapter 33 he chooses the Need.

### What the cruelty is FOR

Not appetite, not sadism, not a scowl. The cruelty is a **substitution
strategy**, and it does one specific job: it converts a problem that needs
a person's consent into a problem that needs only a person's signature.

- He forges the condition report because the alternative is asking Lena for
  a finding she would not give, and asking means she can refuse, and a
  refusal is a fact he cannot append his way around. **Cruelty is what he
  does instead of asking.** Every act of coercion in this book is him
  routing around a possible no.
- It protects him from the thing he cannot survive, which is the firm
  stopping. If the firm stops, the fraud is named, 1951 becomes a crime, and
  his father becomes a criminal instead of a dealer who did one bad Tuesday.
- It proves the Lie: every time a filing holds, the world confirms that
  nothing filed can be unfiled, and he gets to be right.

**If you take the cruelty out:** remove it entirely — make him a hard, cold, rude man
who nonetheless asks — and the book has no adhesion, no Zurich claim, no
March reckoning crisis, no black moment, and Lena goes home in chapter 5.
Chapters 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, 29, 30 and 33 all require
rewriting. Every one of them.

### What he is subject to

- The Deurne Vier: €4.1m, pledged on the claim book, quarterly reckoning,
  three misses and they appoint their own administrator. He has missed one.
- The 1974 deed: he cannot sell, wind up, retire, or refuse the stewardship
  while the pledge is outstanding. Clause 9 is the only door.
- Rachida Bekkali: can strike him off the register on her own authority.
- His own signature: he is registered personally.
- Kasimir Ott, who does not take instructions from anybody else, and who
  will not act without one — which is a form of subjection Sebastiaan does
  not understand until March.

### Three sliders

- **Proactivity 9.** He causes nearly everything in the first half. The
  filing, the removal of Tomas Beke, the disclosure of Armand's report to
  the docket. When he is not acting he is deciding not to, which the ledger
  records as a move.
- **Likability 4.** Deliberately low and it stays low. He is funny about
  money, he is genuinely superb at the work, he is kind to Ruth
  Schindler-Wolff on the telephone, and he does the worst thing in the book
  in chapter 29 with his eyes open. He rises to 5 by the end. He is not
  meant to be safe.
- **Competence 9.** The best provenance researcher in Belgium and not
  modest about it. His incompetence is entirely social: he cannot ask for
  anything, which is the whole engine.

High on two, and the third moves. Antihero profile.

### Arc

**Positive, and narrow.** He does not become good. He becomes a man who
has withdrawn one document. The arc closes in chapter 33 when he does the
one thing his Lie says is impossible — files a corrigendum against himself
— and the closure is verified in chapter 38 by a single behaviour: he asks
Lena a direct question and waits for the answer instead of describing the
conditions under which it might be given.

### Speech pattern (8 dimensions)

1. **Vocabulary level.** High, Latinate, procedural. *Undertaking,
   counterparty, provenance, contingent, instrument, competent authority.*
   He says *acquire* for buy and *dispose* for sell.
2. **Sentence length and structure.** Long, periodic, verb held to the end
   when he is performing. Four to six words when he is not. The drop is the
   tell.
3. **Contractions and formality.** None at all while working — "I do not
   think that is correct." Nothing but contractions when unguarded — "I
   don't know. I didn't think. That's the answer."
4. **Verbal tics.** He prices things inside the sentence. "That is eleven
   days and about forty thousand euro." "This is a Tuesday problem." He
   says *in fact* as a hinge, never as a filler, and it always precedes
   something true he would rather not say.
5. **Question vs statement.** Very low question ratio. He asks perhaps one
   real question a chapter and it is always about the object, never the
   person: "What would you do with it?"
6. **Interruption pattern.** He interrupts by supplying a better noun. If
   you say *glue* he says *hide glue, probably 1960s*. It reads as
   correction and it is also, uncomfortably, always right.
7. **Metaphor domain.** Accounting and conservation, mixed: losses, fills,
   retouching, discount, carrying cost, what a thing is worth held versus
   sold. He describes people as instruments and does not hear himself do it.
8. **Directness.** Deeply indirect. He never asks; he describes the
   circumstances under which a thing would happen and lets the other person
   step into them. "If someone were to sign the annex tonight, the March
   date holds." This is the single most important thing about how he speaks
   and it is the same mechanism as his cruelty, in miniature.

**Example lines.**
- (performing) "The Commission does not remove things. It appends. If you
  find that consoling, you have misunderstood which direction it runs in."
- (performing, chapter 13) "You are describing terms. I am willing to hear
  terms. I would prefer you did not describe them as though I might refuse."
- (unguarded, chapter 26, at the depot door) "Eleven days. I know. Get in
  the van. Please get in the van."
- (unguarded, chapter 31) "I held the lamp. I was nineteen and I was glad
  he asked me."
- (chapter 38, the arc closing) "Do you want to stay. That's the question.
  I'm not going to build a room around it."

### Physical habits and tells

- He cannot produce his own signature cold. He prints his name in block
  capitals on a scrap first, then signs. It started in 1997 and he has
  never examined why. In chapter 33 he files the corrigendum without the
  scrap, and the signature on it is visibly not his usual one, and Rachida
  notices.
- He holds documents at arm's length and lets people read it as contempt.
- When he is lying he becomes more accurate, not less: dates, sums, page
  numbers. Lena works this out in chapter 20.
- He touches the doorframe of the white room and does not come in. Every
  time, for nineteen weeks, until chapter 33.
- He does not sit down in his own house.

### Secrets

1. **The 1997 report is one of nine.** Lucien did it nine times, not once,
   over eleven years, and Sebastiaan has known since 2016 and has told
   nobody — including the Commission, including the Vier, including the four
   families whose pictures were affected. Revealing it would collapse the
   firm's entire back catalogue and is the reason his Lie has to hold.
   (Reader learns chapter 31; Lena learns chapter 34.)
2. **What he gave Lena in chapter 14 was a copy.** He kept the original 1997
   report and let her burn a laser print in a bucket in the yard while he
   watched. He does not tell himself this was a decision. (Reader learns
   chapter 14, Lena chapter 20.)
3. **He knew on 18 March that she was at the depot**, three days in, and did
   nothing until the twenty-fifth. He has an explanation involving the Vier's
   audit window and he knows it is not one. (Reader learns chapter 27.)
4. Minor: the alarm code at Kloosterstraat is 1109, his mother's death date,
   and he has never changed it. Lena uses it to let herself out in chapter 30.

### Relationships

Lucien (father, dead 2016 — the whole wound). Meike (ex-wife, 2018, one
scene in chapter 16, entirely unbitter, which is worse). Kasimir Ott
(confidant, twenty-one years, the only person who calls him by his first
name). Emiel Vandewiele (creditor, and something very close to a second
father, which is why chapter 29 happens in Emiel's kitchen). Rachida
Bekkali (adversary who respects him and is waiting). Lena.

### Thematic role

He embodies the book's question from the side of the ledger that adds: *is
there any repair that is not also a forgery?* He has spent his life making
losses invisible and calling that restitution.

### On the price Sebastiaan pays — design note

I want to be plain about the economics of this arc, because the whole
book stands on it and it would be easy to build a version that cheats.

What Sebastiaan surrenders in chapter 33 is not a feeling and not an
apology. It is the stewardship of the claim book — the office his
grandfather created in 1974 and the only thing three generations of
Corvelijns have ever actually owned. Sixty live claims. Thirty-eight to
forty-four million euro of future commission, signed and retained, walked
into the escrow of the authority he has spent nine years managing. The name
comes off the door of the building his family has traded from since 1951.
He does it in writing, in a corrigendum that states in the first paragraph
that the signature on the Zurich condition report is his forgery, which is a
confession to a criminal offence made voluntarily to a regulator with the
power to refer it — and which does exactly that. The Commission strikes him
from the register of recognised representatives for five years, which in a
trade this small is a professional death sentence; five years is longer than
most claims live. He is forty-one. He will be forty-six.

And he does it at the eighty-seventh percentile of the book, not at the
end, with sixty pages left for him to live inside the consequences rather
than be rescued out of them. That is the test I set myself: could he have
done this and then had the plot hand it back? He could not, because Article
11 runs the same direction for him as it does for Lena. The corrigendum is
on the docket forever. The stewardship, once escrowed under clause 9, cannot
be reclaimed by the resigning steward — that is what makes clause 9 an exit
rather than a manoeuvre. The bar is a published decision. Three
irreversibles, all of them in the world's own currency, all of them
watched: by Rachida, by Kasimir, and by Lena, who is standing in the
registry corridor at Rue de la Loi when it happens and who says nothing.

The counterfeit version of this ending is the one where he makes a speech.
The version I have written costs him the only three things a man in his
position has: the office, the licence, and the name. If a reader finishes
this book unable to say what he lost, I have failed at the level of
sentences, not at the level of design.

---

## 2. Hélène "Lena" Brassart — the constrained lead

**Age 33.** Paper conservator, registration B-4471, ten years qualified.
Adult status established chapter 1: thirty-three, divorced at twenty-nine,
ten years on the register, holds a flat lease in her own name.

**Appearance.** Small, square-shouldered, forearms out of proportion from
years of pressing and lifting. Hair cut short because long hair over a
suction table is a hazard. A white scar across the base of the right thumb
from a scalpel at twenty-two. She dresses for a cold room in a warm month:
two thin layers, always.

### Ghost → Wound → Lie → Want → Need

**GHOST.** Aged twenty-three, home unexpectedly, she came into the kitchen
at eleven at night and found her father rebinding a 1943 German inventory
book at the table, using her own hide glue and her own bone folder, with a
gathering of eight leaves face down that did not belong to it. He looked up
and said, "Put the kettle on." She put the kettle on. She never asked, and
she finished her degree on money she has never accounted for.

**WOUND.** She believes her hands are not hers — that her whole skill came
from a man who used it to lie, and that everything she can do is inherited
stolen goods. Praise makes her ill. She has never entered work under her own
name for anything.

**LIE, in one sentence.** *If the repair is invisible, it is not a lie.*

This is her father's ethic and it is also, precisely, Sebastiaan's, arrived
at from the other end. She works in sympathetic infill: a loss filled so
well that no eye can find it. The profession has been moving away from that
for thirty years toward visible, honest repair, and she has quietly refused
to move with it, and told herself it was craft.

**TRUTH (her Need).** A loss that is filled invisibly is a loss that has
been hidden, and hiding is what happened to all of these pictures in the
first place. She needs to sign something true and let the repair show.

**WANT.** The Academy's Vandenbergh fellowship, deadline 1 June — nine
months to treat and publish the Van der Weyden underdrawing fragment in the
Academy's own collection, under her own name, funded by nobody she owes.
Established in chapter 1, before Sebastiaan exists to her. It is the first
work she would ever have signed.

**Want vs Need in tension:** the Want is a piece of invisible work that
finally has her name on it. The Need requires her to make the repair visible
— to say out loud what was broken. She cannot get the fellowship by telling
the truth about her father, and she cannot tell the truth about her father
and still be the person who deserves the fellowship. She loses the
fellowship in chapter 34 and it does not come back.

### The thing Sebastiaan does not know about her

**She can make paper and ink that will pass a laboratory.** Armand taught
her fibre furnish, sizing, iron-gall recipes and artificial ageing before
she was twenty, as craft, and she has never once used it. Her CV shows
conservation only; the register shows conservation only. He hires her as a
verifier, and she is in fact the only person in Antwerp who could
manufacture the thing he spends his life authenticating.

She uses it once, in chapter 17, on her own initiative, and it changes
everything that follows.

### Three sliders

- **Proactivity 8.** She causes: the refusal in chapter 9 that stalls the
  claim for eleven chapters; the terms in chapter 13; the forged Basel
  receipt in chapter 17; the file handed to Dries Neefs in chapter 23; the
  walk-out in chapter 30; her own statement to the Commission in chapter
  32. Six plot-turning actions, none of them reversed inside the same
  phase.
- **Likability 7.** Dry, exact, bad at being comforted, extremely good at
  the one thing she does. Her cruelty is to her father and it is earned.
- **Competence 9 → 7.** This is the only slider in the book that goes down,
  and it goes down for a physical reason that is never repaired.

### Arc

**Positive.** Lie to Truth. She stops filling losses invisibly. By chapter
36 she is doing visible-repair work at a Rotterdam bindery — tinted fills a
viewer can find, documented, signed — and she is doing it partly because her
hand will no longer let her do anything else, which is the point: her arc is
completed by a subtraction she did not choose and then chosen anyway.

The arc's decisive beat is chapter 32, in Rotterdam, when she decides to go
back to Brussels not for Sebastiaan and not for her father but to file her
own account of what she did in chapter 17 — the first document she has ever
signed that is true and costly at the same time.

### Speech pattern (8 dimensions)

1. **Vocabulary level.** Mid, concrete, technical where technical is
   accurate. Anglo-Saxon and short except for materials, where she is exact
   and unhurried.
2. **Sentence length.** Short and declarative, with the occasional long
   sentence that is always a procedure in order. She does not do
   subordinate clauses about feelings.
3. **Contractions.** Always, in every register, including with the
   Commission. It reads as informality and is actually refusal to perform.
4. **Verbal tics.** She names materials instead of feelings. Asked how she
   is, she says what the humidity is doing. She says "that's not what that
   is" as a complete sentence, roughly twice a chapter.
5. **Question vs statement.** High question ratio, but nearly all of them
   are procedural — "who signed it", "what date", "what's the number" —
   which is how she conducts an interrogation without appearing to.
6. **Interruption pattern.** She interrupts to correct a noun, the same
   move as Sebastiaan's, which is why they are dangerous to each other. The
   difference: he corrects upward into precision, she corrects downward into
   plainness. He says *instrument*; she says *it's a bit of paper*.
7. **Metaphor domain.** Materials, moisture, light, fibre, temperature. She
   thinks about people in terms of what they are made of and how they behave
   wet. **No overlap with his accounting register, and this is enforced:
   she never uses a money word and he never uses a weather word.**
8. **Directness.** Direct to the edge of rudeness, and it gets worse when
   she is frightened.

**Example lines.**
- (chapter 5) "That's my number. That's not my hand. Those aren't the same
  problem and I'd like you to stop talking about them as if they are."
- (chapter 9, the refusal) "No. Not because of the price. Because it isn't
  true and I'd have to look at it under a lamp for the rest of my life."
- (chapter 13, setting terms) "Three things. The 1997 report, in this room,
  today. No door I can't open from the inside. And if you ever put my number
  on anything again I'll walk into Rue de la Loi and take my father with me."
- (chapter 28) "It's a two-micron wobble. You can't see it. I can see it at
  three times and that's the only place it's ever mattered."
- (chapter 38) "I'm not staying because you gave something up. I'm staying
  because I want to and those aren't the same, and you're going to have to
  live with that being the reason."

### Physical habits and tells

- She checks a hygrometer twice in four minutes when she is upset, which is
  not something a person does about the paper.
- She warms her right hand inside her left sleeve without noticing, all
  winter, from the old scaphoid break.
- She smells the corner of a document before she looks at it.
- After the depot: she puts her hand flat on the table before doing anything
  fine, to see. She does this eleven times in the back half of the book and
  it should never be explained.
- She cannot sleep with a door shut. From 26 March onward.

### Secrets

1. **She can forge, to laboratory standard**, and nobody living knows except
   Armand. (Reader learns chapter 17 as it happens; Sebastiaan learns in
   chapter 29, from an auditor, which is the worst possible route.)
2. **She saw her father do it in 2009**, not only in 1997 — twelve years
   after the Kirchner, once more, and she has let both Sebastiaan and the
   Commission believe there was a single incident. This is her own held
   card and it is why she cannot cleanly go to Rachida. (Reader learns
   chapter 21; Rachida learns chapter 32.)
3. She knows who paid her third-year tuition. (Reader learns chapter 34: it
   was Lucien Corvelijn, in 2013, three years before he died, and neither
   Armand nor Sebastiaan has ever mentioned it. Nobody explains it. Nobody
   in this book is going to.)

### Relationships

Armand (father — the wound, the leverage, and the argument). Souad Ferhat
(confidant, and the only person who tells her to stop). Tomas Beke
(colleague; she recommended him for the 2019 Academy loan that got the firm
barred, and his ruin in chapter 11 is partly her doing and she knows it).
Rachida Bekkali (the one who names it). Sebastiaan.

### Thematic role

She embodies the question from the side of the ledger that repairs. She has
spent her life making losses invisible and calling that care.

---

## 3. The Deurne Vier, and Emiel Vandewiele — the body that makes the power real

The consortium is a structure, not a villain. Four investors bought Lucien
Corvelijn's operating debt out of the 2016 estate at fifty-eight cents on
the euro because the claim book was good collateral and the trade was
unglamorous. They want €4.1 million plus eleven per cent. That is the
entire interest and it is completely legitimate. They would go on existing
if Sebastiaan died tonight; they would appoint an administrator by Friday.

**Emiel Vandewiele**, 74, chair. Rope and cordage before he was finance;
the yard is still in the family. Cardiologist since November, which he
mentions exactly twice and never as a bid for sympathy.

- **Ghost:** he lent Lucien Corvelijn 900,000 francs in 1991 on a handshake
  and was repaid in full and early, and it is the only handshake in his life
  that ever went right.
- **Wound:** he has spent thirty years waiting to be that wrong about
  someone again, and cannot tell affection from due diligence any more.
- **Lie:** "A book that balances is a life that was lived correctly."
- **Want:** the €4.1m, on time, and Sebastiaan to be the man Lucien wasn't.
- **Need:** to say plainly that he loved Lucien Corvelijn and was robbed by
  him, and he never does. He dies on 8 May having never said it.
- **Sliders:** proactivity 6, likability 6, competence 8.
- **Arc:** flat, then terminated. He does not change; the world changes
  around his absence.
- **Speech:** short sentences with a long pause in the middle; maritime and
  rope metaphors ("a splice is stronger than a knot and it takes four times
  as long"); no contractions; asks one question and then waits an
  uncomfortable length of time.
- **Secret:** the second schedule to the pledge, which he has never shown
  Sebastiaan, provides that on the chair's death the Vier's controlling vote
  passes to the estate rather than to the remaining three. He wrote it in
  2016 and he wrote it for a reason nobody in this book ever learns.

**Hanne Vandewiele**, 46, his daughter, insolvency lawyer in Ghent. Enters
chapter 16, in force from chapter 34. Wants a clean book for probate and
nothing else; has no view about Sebastiaan whatsoever and finds the sentiment
around the firm faintly embarrassing. Speech: fast, clipped, uses statutory
section numbers in conversation. Competence 9, likability 4, proactivity 7.

---

## 4. Armand Brassart — the leverage, who has his own opinion about it

**Age 71.** Retired paper conservator, Berchem, a first-floor flat with the
tools still on the wall and the bench cleared.

- **Ghost:** February 1997, a diagnosis for his wife Godelieve and a
  treatment in Houston that Belgian insurance would not fund. He signed the
  Kirchner report on a Thursday and she died in 1999 anyway.
- **Wound:** he did the worst thing he has ever done for a reason that
  turned out not to matter, and has been carrying an unpaid invoice ever
  since.
- **Lie:** "The debt is mine and I am the only currency it can be paid in."
- **Want:** to be prosecuted. Genuinely, actively — he wants to be finished.
- **Need:** to understand that his ruin would not settle anything and that
  his daughter is not a payment instrument either.
- **Sliders:** proactivity 4 (he wants to act and his daughter keeps
  stopping him), likability 6, competence 8.
- **Arc:** positive but small and late. He agrees, in chapter 34, not to
  walk in, on the condition that Lena stops treating him as something to be
  protected. It is the least sentimental scene in the book.
- **Speech:** long, courteous, old-fashioned Flemish constructions; uses
  "one" for "you"; the only character who says "shall". Never swears. His
  metaphor domain is weather and gardening, which does not overlap with
  anyone.
- **Example line (chapter 13):** "You are keeping a chair warm for a man who
  would rather stand. Let them have me, Lenneke. I am seventy-one and I have
  been ready since about 2004."
- **Secret:** he did it a second time, in 2009, for a Munch drawing, and
  nobody knows he knows that Lena saw. He is waiting for her to say it
  first. Neither of them ever does.
- **Opinion about being used as leverage:** furious, and directed at Lena,
  not at Sebastiaan. He regards her protection of him as a theft of the only
  meaningful act left to him.

---

## 5. Rachida Bekkali — the one who can name what is happening

**Age 47.** Senior registrar, Commission for the Restitution of Cultural
Property, Rue de la Loi, Brussels. Nineteen years in the registry. She is
not the book's conscience and she is not on anyone's side; she is a civil
servant with a docket and a statutory power she is professionally reluctant
to use.

- **Want:** to close the eleven claims left from the 1998 tranche before she
  retires, because the claimants are dying faster than the counterparties
  are answering.
- **Wound:** her own family's 2004 claim was refused on evidentiary grounds
  and she processed the refusal herself.
- **Sliders:** proactivity 5, likability 6, competence 9.
- **Speech:** complete, unhurried sentences; asks questions to which she
  already has the answer and lets the silence do the work; procedural
  vocabulary used with total precision; never raises her voice; never
  moralises in the abstract, only in the specific.
- **Her plain description, chapter 31 — the line the book is built to
  reach:** "You did not make her lie, Mr Corvelijn. You made her signature
  into a thing you could spend. That is worse, in my office, because a lie
  can be corrected and a signature is the only thing we have."
- **What she does about it:** waits, because striking the firm suspends
  sixty claims; then acts within four hours of the corrigendum landing.

---

## 6. The confidants

### Souad Ferhat — Lena's, 35

Bookbinder, Sint-Andries, third-generation; sister runs a bindery in
Rotterdam. Wants Lena **out** — to leave Antwerp, leave Armand to his fate,
and take the Rotterdam bench. She is not being kind; she thinks the
twenty-two families are a moral bluff Lena has been running on herself.
Speech: fast, interruptive, swears in Dutch, Arabic and French in the same
sentence; metaphor domain is sewing, thread and structure ("you're
oversewing a spine that's already split"). Sliders: proactivity 7,
likability 8, competence 8.

**Her hardest line, chapter 21:** "Twenty-two families is not your
arithmetic. You didn't sign it. You're carrying a bill somebody else ran
up because carrying it is the only way you get to keep him."

### Kasimir Ott — Sebastiaan's, 52

Depot manager, twenty-one years, Lucien's man before Sebastiaan's. Wants
Sebastiaan to **hold** — pay the Vier, close the claim, keep the book. He
regards Lena as an operational exposure and says so. He is not stupid, he is
not sadistic, and he genuinely believes he is doing the necessary thing at
the depot; he brings soup twice a day and keeps a receipt for the camp bed.
Speech: freight and weight metaphors; never finishes a conditional sentence,
which is his single most identifiable feature ("that's the trouble
with —"). Sliders: proactivity 6, likability 5, competence 8.

He resigns in chapter 35 when the book goes to escrow, because there is
nothing left to move. He is not punished. That is deliberate.

---

## 7. Supporting

- **Dries Neefs**, 38, reporter at *De Wacht*. Burned in 2019, careful now,
  will not publish without date-stamps. Not a friend to Lena and says so.
  Publishes 12 March. Speech: rapid, clause-heavy, quotes his own questions
  back.
- **Bram Six**, 61, Commission clerk, on the firm's money since 2013.
  Frightened, mortgaged, apologetic. Not exposed by the end of this book,
  which is on purpose.
- **Tomas Beke**, 36, independent researcher, arrested 6 February on planted
  evidence, charges dropped in April, accreditation not restored. Selling
  secondhand books on Kloosterstraat in chapter 36, four doors from the
  firm. He is not restored. Nobody restores him.
- **Griet Vervoort**, 55, advocaat, Brussels. Two meetings on credit and
  then she stops, which is what actually happens.
- **Ruth Schindler-Wolff**, 88, Basel. The heir on the Zurich claim. She
  appears in person in chapter 36, in Antwerp, and she is not grateful, and
  she is not a lesson. She wants to know why the drawing has a tidemark and
  whether it can be got out.
- **Meike Corvelijn**, 44, Sebastiaan's ex-wife. One scene, chapter 16.
  Entirely without rancour, which is the point of her.
- **Ineke Claes**, 63, cleaner at Kloosterstraat, Tuesdays and Fridays at 6
  a.m. She has a key and she sees things. Chapter 24 depends on her seeing
  one.

---

## Cross-character conflict map

- Sebastiaan wants the claim closed by 31 March. **Lena wants the
  fellowship by 1 June.** Both require her hands and there is not enough of
  her for both. She loses the fellowship.
- Lena wants Armand protected. **Armand wants to be prosecuted.** Direct
  opposition, never resolved by either giving in — they negotiate a third
  thing in chapter 34.
- Kasimir wants Sebastiaan to hold the book. **Souad wants Lena to leave.**
  Both confidants want the opposite of the leads' arcs, and both are, on
  their own terms, correct.
- Emiel wants Sebastiaan to be his father done right. **Hanne wants the
  estate clean.** The father's sentiment and the daughter's balance sheet
  arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions, six weeks apart.
- Rachida wants evidence she can act on. **Dries wants documents he can
  print.** They want the same object for incompatible reasons and never
  meet.
